title: Votes on appointments: who dissents, what fails, and whether donors fare better
question: How did each supervisor vote when an appointment was contested, which nominations did the Board not approve, and did an appointee who had given to a supervisor draw that supervisor’s vote more often than others’?
finding: The Board and its committees took 2,435 roll calls on 1,115 appointment files from 2015 to 2026; 105 were divided (66 of 1,093 at the full Board, 6.0%), the only ones that say anything about one member. Hillary Ronen voted against a nominee most often (20 of 45 divided votes on a nominee). The Board did not approve 39 files (23 tabled or left to lapse, 7 the motion to approve failed, 6 withdrawn, 3 the Board passed a motion rejecting the nomination); 37 of them were the Mayor’s nominations, out of 328 mayoral files. 53 files were continued at least once. On the 23 divided roll calls (21 files, 12 of them the Mayor’s nominations and 4 naming more than one person) where a nominee shared a rare name with an earlier donor to at least one voting member, those members voted for the nominee in 49 of 53 cases (92.5%) and the other members in 111 of 160 (69.4%). Had the recipients voted like the whole Board on each of those roll calls, about 39 of the 53 would have voted for the nominee; shuffling which members were the recipients within each roll call 10,000 times reached 49 or more in 0 shuffles (more than chance would produce). 10 of the donor pairs are confirmed by a second link, and 9 of those voted for the nominee.
how: Every member’s vote on every roll call of the Board’s appointment files, from the appointment download. A roll call is divided when it has at least one aye and one no. A vote counts “on a nominee” when the action approves, recommends or adopts the motion; an aye then favours the nominee, unless the motion’s title rejects the nomination, in which case it is the reverse. Motions to amend, continue, table or divide are counted as divided roll calls but not as votes for or against anyone. “Not approved” covers files whose approving motion failed, files the Board turned into a motion rejecting the nomination, files tabled or left to lapse, and files withdrawn. The donor comparison takes divided votes on a nominee, finds nominees whose rare name appears among contributions to a voting member’s committees dated before the vote, and compares that member’s vote with the other members’ votes on the same roll calls, by keeping each roll call’s votes as they were and shuffling, ten thousand times, which of its voting members count as the recipients. A pair is “confirmed” when the contribution names the occupation as commissioner or its employer is an income source on the nominee’s own Form 700.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. A no vote on a nominee is an ordinary act of oversight, and a supervisor who votes for a nominee who once gave to their campaign may simply know and trust the person: people give to the supervisors they agree with, and contested nominations split the Board along the same lines as its elections, so a gap is expected without any exchange. Nearly all appointment roll calls are unanimous, so the divided ones are few and every per-member figure is small. Some Mayoral nominations take effect if the Board does not act within a deadline, so a file with no Board approval is not always a failed appointment. Names are matched, not identities, and only rare names are used; a multi-person file is treated as one vote on all its nominees. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
